It says 'practice more of this pattern' so you know to schedule another attempt

prompt: Why does a single monotonic counter for generating short-code ids (as used in Tier 2's Cross-Track Capstone #2) break once the URL shortener runs on multiple app servers instead of one?
choices: Base62 encoding only works correctly on a single machine
Multiple servers sharing no coordination can race on the same counter value, producing duplicate codes, or require a shared lock that caps write throughput at one bottleneck
Short codes become too long once traffic increases
Monotonic counters cannot be persisted to disk across a restart

prompt: The single-machine URL shortener needed no cache, but the at-scale version adds a Redis cache-aside layer in front of the database. What's the actual reason the cache earns its place at scale?
choices: Redis is required by law for any production web service
Caches make write operations faster, which is the real bottleneck at scale

Redirect traffic is heavily read-skewed toward recent/popular links, and caching converts 'every redirect hits the database' into 'only cold misses hit the database,' which is what lets read throughput scale past one database's limits
The original Python dict lookup was O(n), and Redis makes lookups O(1) instead

prompt: Why move click-count incrementing off the synchronous redirect request path and into an async queue-and-consumer pipeline at scale?
choices: Databases cannot perform increment operations under any circumstances
The redirect is the most latency-sensitive request in the system, so it should not pay the cost or risk of a synchronous database write just to update a counter the user isn't waiting on
Queues are always faster than direct database writes regardless of load
Click counts are not important data and can be discarded safely

prompt: In the Trapping Rain Water miss example in the tracking log, what was the actual misconception the 'fix_insight' field identified?
choices: The learner used the wrong programming language for the solution

The learner tried to track a single global maximum instead of recognizing that trapped water above each bar depends on the lower of the running max on each side, solvable with two pointers converging from both ends
The learner forgot to import the correct library for array operations
The learner ran out of time before reading the problem statement fully

prompt: In the exercise extending Cross-Track Capstone #2's SlidingWindowLimiter across 5 load-balanced app servers, what specifically breaks if each server keeps its own independent in-memory deque?
choices: The deque data structure stops working correctly above a certain size

A client round-robined across servers is checked against each server's independent count, so the effective limit they experience is close to limit times the number of servers rather than the intended limit
Load balancers cannot route traffic to more than 3 servers at once
Timestamps become inaccurate once more than one process reads the system clock
